Rain began before Nell could plant it. Nell waited under a shelter. When the rain stopped, Nell planted the seed.” Four panels: character and goal / rain problem / waiting response / planting ending. Adapted version: “A robot carried a seed across a moon garden. Its wheel stuck in soft dust. ‘Please help me roll free,’ it called. A friend laid a board across the dust, and the robot reached the planting bed.” This changes character, place, obstacle, response and speech while retaining a goal–difficulty–response–ending structure. Sentence edit: “The robot called” can become “The robot with a long silver arm called from the garden gate.” The added phrases describe which robot and where it calls; these are new fictional details. Out-of-order draft: “Nell planted the seed. The rain stopped. Nell waited under a shelter.” Move the planting after the rain stops, then reread the whole draft. Make your own drawing, words or performance, and show one real edit; naming an edit is not the same as doing it. Digital option with an adult: use an approved drawing or presentation tool to make two original screens titled Problem and Ending. Add your own robot drawings and captions showing the stuck wheel and a coherent rescue. Reorder the screens if needed, change one caption or event to make the connection clearer, then reread the actual revised version. No online sharing is needed.

The children planted six seeds and went back inside.” Before independent reading, the adult may explain the task but should not read the target words or passage to the learner. Practise a different model first. Word cards: planted = plant + ed; seedlings = seed + ling + s; lunchbox = lunch + box. Use known sound–letter patterns, useful word parts and recognised words, checking all printed letters. The suffix ed in planted forms a past action; do not call every frequent word irregular. Phrase practice can group “After lunch” / “the children carried a seed box” / “to the garden”, with other sensible groupings accepted. Controlled adult slip: read “The children planted six seats” while the child sees the actual seeds sentence. Notice seats/seeds mismatch, inspect the letters, repair to seeds and reread for meaning. A prompted repair is recorded separately from a spontaneous self-correction during ordinary reading.

sections.final_normalized_text: Subject-Specific Content & Key Examples2. Subject-Specific Content & Key ExamplesChoose a strategy for the reading needpredict beforevisualise duringmonitor and questionsummarise afterStrategies are tools, not a checklist to use mechanically every time.Build an inferencetext cluewhat I knowreasonable inferencecheck against textAn inference must remain consistent with the evidence.Sort and noticePause at planned points in a short text and name the strategy being used.Guided practiceSort and notice — Pause at planned points in a short text and name the strategy being used.Build or improve — Build inference equations using one text clue plus relevant prior knowledge.Explain your choice — Use the words strategy, literal, inference to explain what you changed and why.Complete story, fact and direction materialStory title: Seeds for the garden. “Nell packed a seed envelope for a train trip. At the station she checked the platform sign. She arrived near the garden just as rain began. Nell put the envelope under her coat and waited under a shelter. When the rain stopped, she planted the seeds.” Before reading, predict possible topic words such as station or garden, then check which actually occur. Literal: Nell waits under a shelter. Inference: keeping the envelope under her coat may protect it from rain; this is supported, not a quoted reason. Visualise the stated place and actions without treating imagined colours as facts. Summary: Nell travels with seeds, waits for the rain to stop, then plants them. Sequence cards: packed seeds / reached rainy garden / waited / planted. Fact card: “Our class planted six seeds on Monday. Four shoots were visible on Friday.” Listen for the stated numbers and days; do not infer that the other seeds can never grow. Directions: draw a rectangle, write Garden inside it, then put a star above it. Listen and follow the actual sequence, ask about an unclear word, and check the finished response. A relevant connection helps understanding; a personal story should not replace the text clues.Original SkillrHub illustration. Words: “The child filled the tray.” The picture adds seeds, a hanging tray and a nearby bird. It does not prove what happens next.Combine the actual picture and wordsRead “The child filled the tray” and inspect the picture supplied here. Seeds pouring into a hanging tray, with a bird nearby, support the inference that it is a bird feeder. The text alone does not identify the tray’s purpose. It does not prove the bird eats next or identify a species. This is evidence discussion, not an instruction to feed wildlife.
